tree-v2.text: Theorem 8.6 . Let ℓ , r , n \ell,r,n be integers such that ℓ + r < n \ell+r<n . The graph compl n ⁡ ( K ℓ , r ) \compl_{n}(K_{\ell,r}) is ensnaring if and only if n − ℓ − r n-\ell-r is odd and ℓ \ell and r r are not both 1 1 . Proof. Let G = compl n ⁡ ( K ℓ , r ) G=\compl_{n}(K_{\ell,r}) . If ℓ = r = 1 \ell=r=1 , then K ℓ , r = K 2 K_{\ell,r}=K_{2} , so Theorem 8.4 tells us that G G is not ensnaring. Henceforth, assume either ℓ \ell or r r is not 1 1 ; we may assume without loss of generality that ℓ ≥ 2 \ell\geq 2 . Let m = n − ℓ − r m=n-\ell-r . We can partition the vertices of G G into sets A = { a 1 , … , a ℓ } A=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{\ell}\} , B = { b 1 , … , b r } B=\{b_{1},\dots,b_{r}\} , and X = { x 1 , … , x m } X=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\} so that every edge is present except those connecting A A and B B . Suppose first that m m is even; we will construct a stone diagram D 0 D_{0} such that the orbit of Θ G \Theta_{G} containing D 0 D_{0} is not contractible. To construct D 0 D_{0} , place the replicas on 𝖢𝗒𝖼𝗅𝖾 n \mathsf{Cycle}_{n} so that • the replicas of vertices in X X appear in the clockwise cyclic order 𝐱 1 , … , 𝐱 m {\bf x}_{1},\ldots,{\bf x}_{m} ; • the replicas of vertices in B B are all in the clockwise arc from 𝐱 m {\bf x}_{m} to 𝐱 1 {\bf x}_{1} ; • the replicas of vertices in A ∖ { a 1 } A\setminus\{a_{1}\} are all in the clockwise arc from 𝐱 1 {\bf x}_{1} to 𝐱 2 {\bf x}_{2} ; • 𝐚 1 {\bf a}_{1} is one space counterclockwise of 𝐛 1 {\bf b}_{1} . Then place the stone so that it coexists with 𝐚 1 {\bf a}_{1} and points toward 𝐛 1 {\bf b}_{1} . Note that D 0 D_{0} is prerefractive and has associated bridged edge a 1 → b 1 a_{1}\to b_{1} . Imagine starting with D 0 D_{0} and iteratively applying Θ G \Theta_{G} . Until the stone sees 𝐱 1 {\bf x}_{1} , the bridged edge will continue to point from A A to B B , and the stone will not turn around. After the stone reaches 𝐱 1 {\bf x}_{1} , the stone coexists with 𝐱 1 {\bf x}_{1} for two steps, and then the stone moves clockwise past 𝐱 1 {\bf x}_{1} . At this time, the bridged edge reverses orientation, and it continues to point from B B to A A until the stone reaches 𝐱 2 \mathbf{x}_{2} . The stone will then move past 𝐱 2 , … , 𝐱 m {\bf x}_{2},\ldots,{\bf x}_{m} in turn, with the bridged edge reversing orientation each time so that afterwards it points from A A to B B . This process will then repeat. The same argument used in the proof of Theorem 8.4 tells us that 𝐱 1 \mathbf{x}_{1} only moves counterclockwise, so the orbit is not contractible. Now suppose m m is odd. Let 𝒪 \mathcal{O} be an orbit of Θ G \Theta_{G} ; we will show that 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is contractible. We may assume there exists a prerefractive stone diagram D ∈ 𝒪 D\in\mathcal{O} since otherwise 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is certainly contractible. Without loss of generality, we can assume the stone coexists with 𝐚 1 {\bf a}_{1} and points clockwise toward 𝐛 1 {\bf b}_{1} in D D . Furthermore, we may assume that if we start at the stone and read the replicas clockwise around the diagram, the replicas of the vertices in X X appear in the order 𝐱 1 , 𝐱 2 , … , 𝐱 m \mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{m} . We claim that 𝒪 \mathcal{O} must contain a post-pivotal stone diagram. Let k k be the smallest positive integer such that the stone points toward 𝐚 1 {\bf a}_{1} in Θ k ​ ( D ) \Theta^{k}(D) . Let k ′ k^{\prime} be the smallest positive integer such that the stone points toward 𝐚 1 {\bf a}_{1} in Θ G k + k ′ ​ ( D ) \Theta_{G}^{k+k^{\prime}}(D) . If Θ G k ​ ( D ) \Theta_{G}^{k}(D) is pre-pivotal and no diagram between Θ k ​ ( D ) \Theta^{k}(D) and Θ k + k ′ ​ ( D ) \Theta^{k+k^{\prime}}(D) is post-pivotal, then there are m m times while we transition from Θ G k ​ ( D ) \Theta_{G}^{k}(D) to Θ G k + k ′ ​ ( D ) \Theta_{G}^{k+k^{\prime}}(D) during which the bridged edge changes whether it points from A A to B B or from B B to A A . Since m m is odd, the bridged edge ends up in the opposite orientation. Hence, when the stone sees 𝐚 2 {\bf a}_{2} again, the resulting stone diagram will be post-pivotal. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the current stone diagram is post-pivotal: after the stone moves 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} past 𝐛 1 \mathbf{b}_{1} , it swaps 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} (we switch ℓ \ell and r r if necessary). The diagrams before and after this swap are nearly conjugates; as a 1 a_{1} and a 2 a_{2} are symmetric vertices, similar to the proof of Proposition 6.1 , we know all replicas except 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} have winding number 0 0 . If, as the stone moves counterclockwise, it encounters any replica of the form 𝐚 i \mathbf{a}_{i} before 𝐱 m \mathbf{x}_{m} , the resulting stone diagram will be post-pivotal. Otherwise, once the stone moves past 𝐱 m \mathbf{x}_{m} , the bridged edge reverses orientation, so if it encounters any replica of the form 𝐛 i \mathbf{b}_{i} before 𝐱 m − 1 \mathbf{x}_{m-1} , the resulting stone diagram will be post-pivotal. This alternating pattern continues. Observe that the stone begins going counterclockwise with 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} right behind it. If the next post-pivotal stone diagram has bridged edge 𝐚 1 → 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{1}\to\mathbf{a}_{2} or 𝐚 2 → 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{2}\to\mathbf{a}_{1} , then it takes two full revolutions of the stone for this to occur. If either 𝐚 3 \mathbf{a}_{3} or 𝐛 2 \mathbf{b}_{2} exists, it is impossible to avoid an earlier post-pivotal stone diagram when the stone passes by this replica in both revolutions. Thus, unless ℓ = 2 \ell=2 and r = 1 r=1 , the next post-pivotal stone diagram’s bridged edge will not involve both 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} . Using the argument from Proposition 6.1 again, we see one of 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} or 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} has winding number 0 0 . As the sum of all winding numbers is 0 0 , we conclude the other has winding number 0 0 as well, so the orbit is contractible. It remains to address the case where ℓ = 2 \ell=2 and r = 1 r=1 . When 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} first swap, 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} swaps clockwise past 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} , and the bridged edge becomes 𝐚 2 → 𝐛 1 \mathbf{a}_{2}\to\mathbf{b}_{1} . The next time the stone sees 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} , the bridged edge has reversed orientation m m times (once for each 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} ), so it is now 𝐛 1 → 𝐚 2 \mathbf{b}_{1}\to\mathbf{a}_{2} . The resulting stone diagram is pre-pivotal, so 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} do not swap, and the bridged edge pivots back to 𝐛 1 → 𝐚 1 \mathbf{b}_{1}\to\mathbf{a}_{1} . The stone then completes another revolution counterclockwise before seeing 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} again, with the bridged edge reversing orientation another m m times to 𝐚 1 → 𝐛 1 \mathbf{a}_{1}\to\mathbf{b}_{1} . This stone diagram is post-pivotal, so 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} swaps counterclockwise past 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} . Thus, every time 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} swaps past 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} , the direction it does so alternates. We conclude that both replicas have the same winding number. The remaining winding numbers are all 0 0 , and the sum of all winding numbers is 0 0 , so 𝐚 1 \mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐚 2 \mathbf{a}_{2} have winding number 0 0 as well. Thus, the orbit is contractible. This proves that G G is ensnaring, as desired. ∎ 9. Future Directions 9.1. Ensnaring Graphs There are still many questions concerning ensnaring graphs that we have not answered. Of course, it would be wonderful to have a complete characterization of ensnaring graphs, though that seems quite difficult at the moment. Here we list some specific problems that could be more manageable. First, let us recall two conjectures that we stated earlier. Conjecture 5.3 says that a wedge of two non-ensnaring graphs is nonensnaring. Conjecture 8.3 says that whether the n n -vertex complement of a fixed graph is ensnaring depends only on the parity of n n . Proving either of these statements would provide very useful structural information about the family of ensnaring graphs. With an eye toward understanding dense graphs, it is natural to ask when the n n -vertex complement of a tree is ensnaring. Conjecture 9.1 . Let T T be an m m -vertex tree, and let n > m n>m be an even integer. Then compl n ⁡ ( T ) \compl_{n}(T) is ensnaring if and only if m m is odd.

planar.text: Conjecture 1.1 . Every planar graph without 3 3 -, 4 4 -, and 6 6 -cycles is ( d 1 , d 2 ) (d_{1},d_{2}) -colorable if d 1 + d 2 ≥ 6 d_{1}+d_{2}\geq 6 . We partially verify the conjecture with the following theorem. Theorem 1.2 . Every planar graph without 3 3 -, 4 4 -, and 6 6 -cycles is ( 2 , 4 ) (2,4) -colorable. Notation and definitions used throughout this work are introduced as follows. A k k -vertex denotes a vertex with a degree of exactly k k , while a k + k^{+} -vertex and a k − k^{-} -vertex refer to vertices with a degree of at least k k and at most k k , respectively. This notation extends similarly to faces. The boundary walk associated with a face f f is denoted by b ⁡ ( f ) b(f) . A vertex v v is said to be incident to a face f f if it lies on the boundary walk b ⁡ ( f ) b(f) . We let N k ​ ( f ) N_{k}(f) denote the number of incident k k -vertices of a face f f .

regular.text: Conjecture 6.2 . Let G G be an n n -vertex regular graph and F ∼ G n , 2 F\sim G_{n,2} be a random 2 2 -regular graph on the same vertex set as G G . Then whp G ∪ F G\cup F is Hamiltonian. As evidence towards this conjecture, note that if G G contains a perfect matching M M (e.g. if G G is one-regular take M = G M=G ) then M ∪ F M\cup F is contiguous to a random cubic graph (see [ 21 , Theorem 9.34] ) so is whp Hamiltonian (see [ 21 , Theorem 9.20] ). If G G is regular of even degree then G G contains a 2 2 -factor (Petersen’s Theorem), so this case would follow from the 2 2 -regular case; a first step here is a result of Frieze [ 17 ] that the union of two random 2 2 -factors is whp Hamiltonian. For the general conjecture, by Hall’s theorem any regular graph G G contains a spanning subgraph H H where each component is a cycle or an edge, so it would suffice to show for any such H H that whp H ∪ F H\cup F is Hamiltonian.

tangency.text: Conjecture 2 . Every set of n n pairwise intersecting bi-infinite x x -monotone k k -intersecting curves admits O k ​ ( n ) O_{k}(n) tangencies. We were unable to settle this conjecture. Still, we mention a simple and weak polynomial upper bound and two observations regarding the conjecture. For the upper bound we use the following observation. Observation 1 . Let r r and r ′ r^{\prime} be two bi-infinite x x -monotone curves touching from below an x x -monotone curve b b . Then r r and r ′ r^{\prime} cross at a point whose x x -coordinate is between b ∩ r b\cap r and b ∩ r ′ b\cap r^{\prime} . By Theorem 1 we have O k ​ ( n 2 − 1 k + 3 ) O_{k}\left(n^{2-\frac{1}{k+3}}\right) tangencies among any n n k k -intersecting curves. One can slightly improve upon this bound in case of bi-infinite x x -monotone curves.
